extracted.intended_audience: lay students and general readers studying philosophy of science / scientific method
extracted.subtask_description: Clarifying what counts as a scientific law and what the scientific method requires: how facts are classified, compared, and condensed into brief formulas meaningful to human thought. Emphasizes limits of knowledge relative to human perceptive faculties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific method — classification, comparison, and formulation
rubrics_metrics.description: The scientific method consists in the careful and often laborious classification of facts, in the comparison of their relationships and sequences, and finally in the discovery by disciplined imagination of a brief statement or formula which in a few words resumes the whole range of facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classification is not identical with mere collection: it denotes the systematic association of kindred facts, the collection not of all facts but of relevant and crucial facts. The formula discovered serves the economy of thought by permitting fitting exertion with minimum thought upon receipt of new sense-impressions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific law as a brief statement or formula
rubrics_metrics.description: A scientific law (or formula) is a brief statement or formula which resumes the relationship between a group of facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such a formula condenses a vast number of observed sequences into a mental shorthand; for example, Newton's law is the invention of a method of briefly describing planetary motion in terms of a mental conception (mutual acceleration). The author prefers 'formula' to avoid confusion with juridical senses of 'law'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific law is descriptive, not prescriptive
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific law describes relationships among perceptions and conceptions; it does not command or prescribe conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast with civil/moral law (which implies command and duty). Confusing the descriptive scientific sense with the prescriptive juridical/moral sense leads to conceptual muddiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laws must be grounded in sense-impressions and mental conceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific laws relate to perceptions and conceptions formed by human perceptive and reasoning faculties; they are the resume or brief expression of relationships and sequences among those perceptions and conceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The law involves an association of natural phenomena with mental conceptions lying outside the particular field of those phenomena; without the mental conceptions the law could not exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowledge and law are meaningful only within the sphere of human thought
rubrics_metrics.description: The term 'knowledge' is meaningless when extended beyond the sphere in which we may legitimately infer consciousness or beyond the plane of human thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No inference is legitimate which carries thought beyond nervous systems akin to human beings. Attempts to assert knowledge of 'things-in-themselves' or unthinkable entities are idle and unmeaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural law is relative to the perceiver's faculties
rubrics_metrics.description: What we call natural law is conditioned by human perceptive and retentive faculties; a being with different or sharper faculties might perceive different regularities and for it some of our laws (e.g., the Second Law of Thermodynamics) might not hold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by Clerk-Maxwell's demon: our thermodynamic laws summarize human-scale experience; beings who can track individual molecules would conceive 'nature' differently. The law's 'universal' validity must be read relative to a certain type of perceptive faculty (normal human beings).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sequences of observations are not laws until classified and generalized
rubrics_metrics.description: A repeated sequence of sense-impressions (observations) is not in itself a law; classification, comparison with other sequences, generalization, and the formation of mental conceptions are required before a concise law-worthy statement can be made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even exhaustive descriptions of planetary motions or other phenomena do not constitute a law until summarized by a concise formula that unifies those sequences. Historical continuity of sequences does not equal formulation of law.

rubrics_metrics.name: A scientific law comes into existence when formulated by human intellect
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific law owes its existence to the creative power of human intellect: the statement of a formula is the creation (not merely discovery) of the law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While sequences of phenomena may have occurred prior to formulation, the law (as a mental shorthand linking conception and phenomena) exists only when humans associate the conception with the phenomena and express it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use 'law' with caution — distinguish its multiple senses
rubrics_metrics.description: The word 'law' has multiple senses (scientific/formulaic, juridical/command-based, and the mere sequence of phenomena) and conflating them causes confusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors and readers should take care to indicate which sense is meant; historical and philosophical arguments often err by shifting among these senses (examples: Stoics, Hooker, Austin). Prefer 'formula' when speaking scientifically if confusion is likely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universal validity of scientific law is qualified
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific laws have universal validity only in so far as they apply to a certain type of perceptive faculty — namely, normal human beings with unmodified perceptive and reasoning faculties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thus 'universal' should be interpreted as universal across normal humans and not as validity independent of any perceiver or for beings with very different faculties.
